clue.text: Autographs from inferior writers …

parts.note: sub- means below or lesser, as in substandard
scribes are people who write things out

explanation.surface: Signatures collected from second-rate authors, running on into the next clue's verdict on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Autographs' reads as a plural noun but is the verb: someone who autographs a document signs it.
explanation.definitionFit: To subscribe a document is to sign one's name at its foot, which is what autographing does.

clue.text: Crack unit with hard belt

parts.note: the Special Air Service, the elite British army regiment
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A crack army unit equipped with a tough belt.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is a band of cloth worn round the waist or over the shoulder, a kind of belt.

clue.text: Conference section possibly, according to Spooner, not a safe place to be

definitions.text: not a safe place to be

indicators.note: Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so the starts are exchanged

parts.note: Conference is a common variety of pear and a section is a bit; Spooner swaps the opening sounds

explanation.surface: A slice of some conference, maybe, is a dangerous spot to be in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conference' looks like a meeting but is the pear variety; swapping the first sounds of PEAR BIT gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bear pit is figuratively a hostile, rowdy arena, so a place where you are not safe.

clue.text: Touch left sense around — these will enhance another

indicators.note: around suggests being turned about, so the letters of the word are moved into a different order

parts.note: contact means touch
L is the abbreviation for left
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Touch is a sense, and these things improve a different sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' refers back to 'sense' in the surface: the senses are touch and sight, and the answer improves sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Contact lenses sit on the eye to correct vision, so they enhance the sense of sight.

clue.text: Cockney's innuendo finished off fiancée

indicators.note: a Cockney accent famously drops the aitch at the start of words

parts.note: an innuendo is an indirect hint
ended means finished

explanation.surface: An East Ender's suggestive remark finishes off his bride-to-be.
explanation.walkthrough: HINT loses its H as a Cockney would say it, giving INT.
explanation.definitionFit: One's intended is the person one is engaged to marry, a fiancée.

clue.text: Record number cycling final parts of Le Tour

indicators.note: cycling moves letters round in a loop, so the first letter goes to the back

parts.note: ten is a number

indicators.note: the final parts of words are their last letters

parts.note: the last letters of Le and Tour

explanation.surface: A record number of riders cycling the closing stages of the Tour de France.
explanation.walkthrough: TEN with its first letter moved to the end becomes ENT. 'cycling' fits the Tour de France surface but works as the device.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter something is to record it in a log or register.

clue.text: … prove ultimately worthless by the way

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very end, so only the closing letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the final letter of worthless
how is the way or manner by which something is done

explanation.surface: Continuing 1 Across: the autographs of bad writers turn out to be worth nothing, as an aside.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots join this clue to 1 Across, so the surface runs on from it; 'prove' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To show something is to demonstrate it, establishing it as true just as proving does.

clue.text: Desperado played to death, hit finally replaced by Henley's opener

indicators.note: something played is performed in a new way, so the letters are rearranged
replaced by tells us one letter is swapped out for another

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finally picks out the closing letter of the word before it

parts.note: the last letter of hit

indicators.note: an opener is what comes first, so only the initial letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of Henley

explanation.surface: The Eagles' song Desperado, co-written by Don Henley, overplayed until the hit wore thin.
explanation.walkthrough: One T of TO DEATH becomes H, and the resulting letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A hothead is a reckless, impetuous person, much like a desperado who acts without regard for danger.

clue.text: Sweeping extra delivery at Lord's over cover

indicators.note: in a down entry, over means placed above, which sets the order of the parts

parts.note: in cricket a wide is a ball out of the batter's reach, which counts as an extra run; Lord's is the London cricket ground
a spread is a bedcover

explanation.surface: A cricket picture: a wide ball sent down at Lord's flying past the fielder at cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' and 'cover' both look like cricket terms here (an over is six balls; cover is a fielding position), but 'cover' is the bedspread.
explanation.definitionFit: Widespread means extending over a large area, as does sweeping in the sense of wide-ranging.

clue.text: Bridge across India and another country

indicators.note: a bridge stretching across something has it inside its span, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a span is a bridge or the arch of one
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A bridge spanning India and some neighbouring nation.
explanation.walkthrough: SPAN wraps round I to give SPAIN; 'another' fits because India itself is a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain is a nation, and the clue calls it another country because India has already appeared.

clue.text: Made up two appeals over tax credit, having lost case twice

indicators.note: turned over means flipped round, so the pair of appeals is read from the end back
a case is the outer layer, so losing it twice strips the end letters on both sides two times

parts.note: IT is sex appeal, taken twice
value added tax, the UK sales tax
taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: Someone made up a story about lodging two appeals on a tax credit ruling and losing both.
explanation.walkthrough: CREDIT loses its outer letters to give REDI, then again to give ED. 'Made up' looks like 'invented' but means applied cosmetics.
explanation.definitionFit: To titivate is to smarten one's appearance, often with cosmetics, so a titivated face has been made up.

clue.text: Failing to get parking depressing one in home and one in office

indicators.note: pressing down on something means sitting on top of it, which in a down entry fixes which part comes first

parts.note: a vice is a moral failing
P is the road-sign symbol for parking
a resident is someone living in a home

explanation.surface: Not finding a parking space, depressing for both a householder and an office worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depressing' looks like an adjective but means P presses down on RESIDENT. 'office' means public post, not a workplace.
explanation.definitionFit: A vice-president holds a high office, deputising for the president, so is one in office.

clue.text: Snacks, possibly wrap and noodles to begin with

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters could be rearranged into another form, and the answer's second word says how

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to begin with points to the start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of noodles
crackers is itself an anagram signal, so the second word spells out what possibly asks for

explanation.surface: Choosing a starter at a takeaway: perhaps a wrap, with some noodles first.
explanation.walkthrough: Read cryptically, the answer is an instruction: its first word is the other letters gone crackers, i.e. scrambled. This is a reverse clue, where the answer supplies the device.
explanation.definitionFit: Prawn crackers are light crisp fried snacks flavoured with shrimp, served with Chinese food.

clue.text: Fit of pique shown by the French after abrupt holiday changes

indicators.note: abrupt means cut off suddenly, so the word loses its last letter
after means following, which sets which pieces come first in the answer

parts.note: a rest is a break or holiday
a huff is a fit of bad temper
les is French for the (plural)

explanation.surface: French tourists sulk after their trip is cut short by a change of plans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holiday' comes last in the clue but first in the answer, as 'after' says. 'changes' is a noun here, as in cabinet reshuffles.
explanation.definitionFit: Reshuffles are reorganisations, notably of a cabinet, so they are changes.

clue.text: Shy of masculine guys designated as eligible

indicators.note: shy of means short of or lacking, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: guys are men
M is the grammatical abbreviation for masculine
titled means given a name or title

explanation.surface: Timid about macho blokes who have been labelled as good catches.
explanation.walkthrough: MEN without its M leaves EN, followed by TITLED.
explanation.definitionFit: Being entitled to something means having the right or qualification for it, so eligible.

clue.text: Rest of papers taken by counter agents

indicators.note: something taken by another is held inside it
counter means running against, so the word for agents goes the opposite way

parts.note: reps are sales representatives, agents of a firm
identity papers, ID

explanation.surface: The remainder of the documents was seized by spies working against us.
explanation.walkthrough: REPS reversed is SPER, which takes in ID. In snooker a rest is a stick used to support the cue, and a spider is a raised version of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A spider is a type of snooker rest with tall legs that lets the cue pass over another ball.

clue.text: General de Gaulle's refusal to accept a fellow European

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so the other pieces go inside

parts.note: non is French for no, as de Gaulle famously said to British entry to the EEC
taken as written
a Pole is a European from Poland

explanation.surface: De Gaulle refused to let another European country in, as he did Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: De Gaulle twice vetoed Britain's entry to the European Economic Community with a famous 'non'. 'General' is the definition, not a description of de Gaulle.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French general before he became emperor.

clue.text: Boost assuming hotel is given new mark

indicators.note: to assume is to take on, so one piece takes another into itself

parts.note: hype is publicity that boosts something
H for hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A hotel gets a new rating after a promotion campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: HYPE takes H inside to make HYPHE, then N follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A hyphen is a punctuation mark joining words or parts of words.

clue.text: Garden largely split up to display better half

indicators.note: largely means mostly but not all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a park is a large public garden

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: rent means split or torn

explanation.surface: A garden mostly divided up to show off the nicer half.
explanation.walkthrough: 'split up' looks like one phrase but 'up' only turns RENT round. 'better half' looks like part of the garden but is the spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: One's better half is a jocular term for a spouse or partner.

clue.text: City cave in, somehow Arsenal's wingers penetrating

indicators.note: somehow suggests things are done in some unspecified way, so the letters are rearranged
penetrating means getting inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: these six letters rearranged

indicators.note: wingers play at the edges of a team, so the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of Arsenal

explanation.surface: A football report: the city side's defence collapses as Arsenal's wide players break through.
explanation.walkthrough: AL goes inside the rearranged letters after the V.
explanation.definitionFit: Valencia is a large city on the east coast of Spain.

clue.text: Gent regularly seen wearing Mac perhaps close to college — it could be related

indicators.note: something wearing a garment has it around it, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a mac (mackintosh) is a type of coat

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the first and third letters of Gent

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its final letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter of college

explanation.surface: A gentleman in a raincoat often spotted near a college could be a relative.
explanation.walkthrough: A mac is a mackintosh, a British word for a raincoat. 'regularly' here takes the odd letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A cognate is a word or thing sharing a common origin with another, so something that is related.

clue.text: Promising pro gaining points had to be paid

parts.note: pro means in favour of, for
E and S, two compass points
HAD plus OWING, which means due to be paid

explanation.surface: A promising professional picked up points but had to pay up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'had to be paid' splits as HAD + OWING; 'gaining' simply joins FOR to the points.
explanation.definitionFit: Something foreshadowing a future event hints at or promises it in advance.

clue.text: Lady Gaga's bottom trimmer, wouldn't you say?

indicators.note: the bottom of a word in a down entry is its final letter

parts.note: the last letter of Gaga

indicators.note: asking what you would say points to the sound of the words when spoken

parts.note: neater means trimmer, tidier

explanation.surface: Lady Gaga's backside is slimmer, don't you think?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lady' is the definition, split off from Gaga's name; A plus NEATER, spoken in a non-rhotic accent, gives the woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Anita is a woman's name, and a lady is a woman.

clue.text: Uplifted, bumped into one or two people sleeping together?

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: uplifted in a down entry means turned to read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to bump into someone is to meet them by chance

explanation.surface: Elated after running into someone special, perhaps a couple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uplifted' reads as elated but turns the word upside down in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is informal for a couple in a romantic relationship; the question mark flags the indirect description.

clue.text: Country's idle put to work shifting earth

indicators.note: putting something to work sets it in motion, so the letters are moved into a new order

parts.note: land is a country, with the possessive S
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A nation's layabouts are set to work moving soil.
explanation.definitionFit: A landslide is a mass of earth and rock sliding down a slope, earth on the move.

clue.text: Pass time, stick around

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way, so the word for stick runs backwards

parts.note: a cane is a walking stick
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Kill time by idling with a walking stick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass time' looks like one phrase; 'Pass' is the definition, in the parliamentary sense, and the stick is placed before the time.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass a law is to enact it, making it legally binding.

clue.text: Agent Mulder's back on board and perky

indicators.note: something on board is inside the vessel, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a spy is a secret agent

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only its final letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter of Mulder

explanation.surface: Fox Mulder of The X-Files returns to the team in lively form.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes inside SPY.
explanation.definitionFit: Spry means lively and active, especially for an older person, so perky.

clue.text: Customary of course to sit behind premier

indicators.note: sitting behind something means coming after it, which fixes the order of the two parts

parts.note: main means chief or principal
a stream is a watercourse

explanation.surface: It is normal, naturally, for a deputy to sit behind the prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally', but 'course' is the running water.
explanation.definitionFit: Mainstream describes what is conventional and normal, the usual or customary way.
